Well, they sent me here. It wasn't really my idea to come, you know? I'm an EMT, I work out of Station 42, and yesterday we had this shift... it started out okay, I guess, but then I was in the bay with the rigs, and the airway bags—the blue ones, you know the ones we use for intubation and all that—they just weren't right. The way they were sitting on the shelves, it was all wrong. So I started moving them. I had to put them into a specific pattern, a pattern I just *knew* was right. "Unit 42, respond to a 10-54," over and over, because the numbers had to match the pattern I was making with the bags. 

My lieutenant, he came in and saw me, and he told me to stop. He said, "Hey, what are you doing with the gear? Step away." But I couldn't. I just couldn't step away. If I broke the sequence, if I stopped moving the bags or stopped saying the numbers, it felt like the whole bay—the rigs, the equipment, everything—would just go bad. Like something terrible would happen if the pattern wasn't finished. So I kept doing it, and he kept yelling, and then... well, they said I wasn't fit to be on shift and told me I had to come here. But I was just trying to keep everything from going bad, you know? The sequence was important.

Well, it’s... it’s not really a choice between the two, it’s both, but the worry is so big it swallows everything else. I mean, you have to understand the layout of Station 42. We have three rigs parked in there, and the equipment shelves are right along the back wall. When I was looking at those blue airway bags—and these are the main trauma bags, the ones with the laryngoscopes and the ET tubes, very critical gear, you know?—when I started moving them, it was because the space around them felt completely unstable. 

So I knew the pattern. I knew exactly how they had to sit, the exact angles. But the feeling... the feeling was like this massive, crushing pressure in the air. If I didn't get them into that exact pattern, and if I didn't keep repeating those dispatch numbers out loud—like I said, "Unit 42, respond to a 10-54," over and over, exactly the way the dispatcher's voice sounded earlier that morning—if I didn't do both of those things at the exact same time, the whole bay was going to go bad. 

And I don't mean just a little bad. I mean the rigs, the concrete floor, the oxygen tanks, the fluorescent lights, everything was going to turn wrong. Like it would all just rot or collapse or become completely toxic. That's why when my lieutenant came in and started yelling at me to step away from the gear, I just couldn't do it. I wouldn't step away. He was getting so mad, telling me to stop, but he didn't see that I was the only thing keeping the room together. If I broke the sequence to listen to him, if I stopped talking or stopped moving my hands, the whole place would have gone bad right then and there. So I just kept moving the bags and saying the numbers, and that's exactly why they forced me to come here, because they didn't understand I was actually protecting the station.

Well, I mean, if you're asking if I've ever had to arrange the airway bags exactly like that before, no, that specific sequence in the bay was yesterday. But... well, the way things have been, the way the station feels, and the other things I've had to do to manage it, that's been happening for a while. Not forever, but... I noticed it right away. And then the paperwork, the run reports we have to fill out on the tablets—the forms started looking different to me. Not the words, but the spaces between the words. They were holding too much weight, if that makes sense. Like they were heavy. So I had to start tracing the edges of the tablet screen with my thumb before I could hit submit, just to ground the data so it wouldn't, you know, corrupt the dispatch system. 

And my partner, Dave, he started giving me these looks. He’d be driving, and I'd be in the passenger seat, tracing the screen, and he’d ask if the tablet was frozen. But I couldn't explain it to him, because if I talked while I was tracing, the grounding wouldn't work. So I just had to ignore him. That’s been going on for about eight weeks, I guess. The camera lenses watching, the heavy spaces on the forms, and then yesterday, the airway bags in the bay... it’s all connected to the same shift in the environment. It’s all been building up over these last two months, culminating in what happened yesterday when my lieutenant decided to make a huge deal out of me just trying to keep the station from going bad. So, yeah, the specific bag thing was new, but the... the need to manage the environment, the cameras and the paperwork, that's been the last two months.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Control events or people? Like, with my mind? No. I mean... no, of course not. That sounds like something out of a comic book or a sci-fi movie. I don't have special powers. 

You're probably asking that because of what I said about the tablet, right? The grounding? But you have to understand the difference between what I'm doing and what you're asking. I am not controlling the tablet in some abnormal, magical way. It's an electronic device. It runs on circuits and batteries, and when the spaces between the words get too heavy—because of the interference from the cameras and what the supervisors are doing on the server—it creates a physical instability. When I trace the edge of the screen with my thumb, I am physically interacting with it. I am completing a circuit to ground the data. Anyone could do it if they actually paid attention to the shift in the environment. It's not some special ability that *I* have, and I'm certainly not doing it just by thinking about it. I have to physically do the work. 

And as for controlling people? God, I wish I could. If I could control people, do you think I'd let the injury review board go into the server and alter my patient care reports? If I could just think a thought and make people behave differently, I would have made my lieutenant stop making such a huge deal out of me securing the bay yesterday. I would have made him see the reality of the situation. But I can't. I can't control them at all. I'm completely at their mercy when it comes to what they decide to do behind a desk. All I can do is react to it. 

When I arrange the airway bags, I'm not controlling the supervisors. I'm just... I'm securing the physical space. It's exactly like putting a deadbolt on a door. When you lock your front door at night, you aren't controlling the people outside, you're just making sure they can't get in and mess with your stuff. That's all I'm doing. So, no. I don't have any weird beliefs about controlling computers with my thoughts or making people do things. I'm just an EMT, trying to use basic, physical principles to keep my station from going bad while management tries to sabotage my career.

Are we... didn't we just cover this basically? Putting thoughts into my mind? Making me do things against my will? No. No, absolutely not. I feel like you're asking the same thing but just using different words, and I'm going to give you the exact same answer. My mind is my own.

My thoughts are entirely generated by my own brain. I took anatomy and physiology—twice, actually, because the first professor at the community college completely skimmed over the central nervous system and I needed to know the actual mechanics of it for my clinicals. So I know how neurotransmitters work. I know how synapses fire. When I am sitting in the passenger seat of the rig, looking at the MDT—the Mobile Data Terminal—and I think to myself, "I need to document the exact time this patient's respiratory rate dropped," that is my thought. That is my clinical judgment based on my training. No one is beaming that into my head. 

The problem isn't what's going into my mind. The problem is what they are doing to my documentation after it leaves my mind and goes into the server. Do you see the difference? It's a completely external threat. They aren't tampering with my brain, they're tampering with the digital dispatch system.

I willed myself to trace the edge of the screen to fix the heavy spaces between the words. No one is forcing my muscles to move. No one is planting ideas in my head like some kind of telepathy or... or microchip nonsense. I deal in facts, and the fact is, my mind is completely my own. It's actually the only thing they haven't been able to tamper with, which is exactly why they have to resort to changing my patient care reports behind my back to make me look crazy. So, no. I mean, you have to understand the layout of Station 42. We have three rigs parked in there, and the equipment shelves are right along the back wall. When I was looking at those blue airway bags—and these are the main trauma bags, the ones with the laryngoscopes and the ET tubes, very critical gear, you know?—when I started moving them, it was because the space around them felt completely unstable. \n\nSo I knew the pattern. I knew exactly how they had to sit, the exact angles. But the feeling... the feeling was like this massive, crushing pressure in the air. If I didn't get them into that exact pattern, and if I didn't keep repeating those dispatch numbers out loud—like I said, \"Unit 42, respond to a 10-54,\" over and over, exactly the way the dispatcher's voice sounded earlier that morning—if I didn't do both of those things at the exact same time, the whole bay was going to go bad. \n\nAnd I don't mean just a little bad. I mean the rigs, the concrete floor, the oxygen tanks, the fluorescent lights, everything was going to turn wrong. Like it would all just rot or collapse or become completely toxic. That's why when my lieutenant came in and started yelling at me to step away from the gear, I just couldn't do it. I wouldn't step away. He was getting so mad, telling me to stop, but he didn't see that I was the only thing keeping the room together. If I broke the sequence to listen to him, if I stopped talking or stopped moving my hands, the whole place would have gone bad right then and there. So I just kept moving the bags and saying the numbers, and that's exactly why they forced me to come here, because they didn't understand I was actually protecting the station.\n\nDoctor: While you were arranging the airway bags and repeating the dispatch numbers, were you having thoughts that you couldn’t control or didn’t want, like a fear that something terrible would happen if you stopped?\n\nPatient: Well, no, it's not like that. It wasn't... I wasn't having thoughts I didn't want, or thoughts I couldn't control. It wasn't some kind of, you know, intrusive fear just popping into my head out of nowhere. It was a fact. It was a reality of the situation in the bay at that exact moment. \n\nSee, you're making it sound like I was just sitting there worrying, like I was scared of something happening, but it wasn't a worry. It was a physical certainty. The air in the bay—and this is a big space, you have to remember, high ceilings, lots of echo, the smell of diesel and bleach—the air itself was changing. I wasn't trying to fight off some random thought about things going bad. I was actively managing the environment. The numbers, the dispatch codes, the specific placement of those blue airway bags... I was in complete control of what I was doing. I had to be. \n\nIf I wasn't in control, if I was just having random thoughts, I wouldn't have been able to keep the sequence going when my lieutenant started yelling. I mean, he was really loud, his voice bouncing off the concrete, but I didn't lose focus. I didn't let my mind wander to what he was saying or get scared by him. I stayed completely dialed into the pattern. So, no, it wasn't unwanted thoughts. It was exactly what I needed to be thinking and doing to keep the whole station from going completely wrong. I was entirely focused on the task.\n\nDoctor: Has anything like this ever happened to you before, or was this the first time you felt this way?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean, if you're asking if I've ever had to arrange the airway bags exactly like that before, no, that specific sequence in the bay was yesterday. I even brought it up to them! I brought the tablet right to my supervisor and showed him that the data had been altered, and he just... he completely lied to my face. He gave me this patronizing look and told me it's just routine paperwork, that the system just auto-formats things sometimes. Auto-formats! Two solid months. \n\nAnd I say 'alarmed' because that's the word my lieutenant actually used, which is just... it's a massive overreaction. Me securing the bay and grounding the tablets shouldn't alarm anyone who actually understands what's happening. But for the last two months, it’s like I’m speaking a completely different language to them. I try to explain how the cameras are causing that physical instability I told you about, and how the supervisors are tampering with the paperwork on the server to frame me, and they just look at me like I'm the one who doesn't make sense. \n\nIt started right around the time they recalibrated the security feeds in the bay, exactly two months ago. Ever since then, day in and day out, I've been the only one trying to keep the environment stable. And sure, maybe they don't share my understanding of it. Maybe my thinking is different from theirs, but only because I'm actually paying attention to the details! I'm looking at the MDT, I'm seeing the heavy spaces between the words, I'm tracking the discrepancies in the patient care reports that the injury review board keeps altering. \n\nYou asked if this happens outside the job, but... being a medic, having that level of situational awareness, it doesn't just turn off when my shift ends. You don't just leave that at the station. I take that awareness everywhere. So yes, for the last two months, I've been entirely alone in seeing what's really going on with the cameras and the paperwork, and everyone else is just... they're just completely blind to it, and they act like I'm the problem for actually doing something about it.\n\nDoctor: Have you believed, at any point during these past two months, that the changes you noticed in the environment — like the camera angles or altered paperwork — were specifically targeted at you, rather than happening randomly or to others as well?\n\nPatient: Randomly? To others? No, no, no. Look, I talk to the other guys on B-shift. I talk to Miller, I talk to Davis... well, I used to, before they started looking at me sideways. But their MDTs aren't doing this. Their reports aren't getting flagged. It is specifically, one hundred percent, targeted at me. \n\nI know for an absolute fact that the injury review people—and... and some of the supervisors, too—they have been watching me through those station cameras. That recalibration two months ago? That wasn't for general security. That was so they could get a better angle on the bay exactly where I park the rig, and on the desk exactly where I sit to do my charting. They sit there and they watch me, and then the second I hit submit on my triage notes... they go into the server and they change them. They actually alter the raw data. \n\nLike, I'll write that a patient had clear bilateral lung sounds and a normal respiratory rate, and suddenly the file is changed to make it look like I completely missed a crucial airway compromise. They are deliberately changing my triage notes to make me look unsafe. To make it look like I'm a danger to the public and shouldn't have my patch! \n\nAnd the absolute most frustrating part of this whole thing... the part that just makes my blood boil... is that when I bring it up, when I marched into the supervisor's office last week and demanded to know why my triage narratives were completely rewritten, you know what they told me? They looked me dead in the eye, with this condescending little smirk, and told me it's just \"routine paperwork.\" Routine paperwork! They said, \"Oh, we're just doing routine QA/QI, quality assurance, just cleaning up the formatting for the state database.\" \n\nCleaning up the formatting doesn't change a respiratory rate from 16 to 8! It doesn't! They hide behind this... this bureaucratic wall, telling me it's just routine paperwork, but I know exactly what they're doing. They're building a file on me. They are watching my every move on those cameras, waiting for me to do something they can twist, and when I don't give them anything because my clinical skills are rock solid, they just change the notes themselves to make me look incompetent. So no, doctor, this isn't some random system glitch or something happening to the whole station. It is a highly coordinated, specific attack on my license by the injury review board.\n\nDoctor: Have you believed, for at least a month at a time, that these things were happening—like the cameras watching you and your reports being changed—even when there was no evidence to support it?\n\nPatient: Evidence? Wait, what do you mean, no evidence? I feel like you're completely missing what I just explained to you. I just laid out the evidence! \n\nYou say 'no evidence,' but I... I know what I'm seeing. It’s not a guess, it’s not just some passing thought, it’s a documented fact. I know for an absolute certainty that the injury review people, and like I said, some of the shift supervisors too, have been watching me through those station cameras. I can literally see the little red indicator light on the dome camera in the bay shifting when I walk past the decon room. It tracks me. I'll be doing my morning rig checks, counting the airway adjuncts, and I can feel them watching my hands. They tell me it's just routine paperwork! I wouldn't step away. I absolutely refused to step away when my lieutenant told me to stop because I knew, I knew for an absolute fact, that if I broke the sequence before it was finished, the whole bay would go bad. The rigs, the gear, the whole station environment would just be completely compromised and unsafe. \n\nBut he did not understand cause and effect at that level. He just saw me moving the airway bags into a pattern and repeating the numbers, and instead of realizing I was stabilizing the room, he pulled me off duty and sent me here to this hospital. So yes, my actions influence the environment, but it is a necessary protocol. They just look at me with these blank faces and tell me it is just routine paperwork. Routine paperwork! As if changing a patient vital sign or my narrative about airway management is just some standard administrative clerical update. It is not! It is deliberate sabotage to make me look like a danger to my patients. So no, I do not doubt myself for a single moment, because I am living in reality, and the reality is that they are doing this to me every single day. I know what I see, and I know exactly what they are doing.\n\nDoctor: In the past two months, have you believed in any other threats or conspiracies beyond the injury review board changing your reports and the cameras watching you?\n\nPatient: Other threats? Isn't it enough that I know the injury review people and some of the supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras? Because that alone—just that one thing, the constant surveillance, the feeling of those lenses tracking every single move I make in the bay while I'm trying to do my inventory—that is a massive violation of my privacy and my professional space. It's all-consuming. \n\nI haven't needed to look for other conspiracies because the one happening right in front of my face is destroying my life! They are changing my triage notes to make me look unsafe. That's the threat! That is the only threat that matters right now. The interventions are altered. And they do this specifically to build a case against me, to make me look like I don't know what I'm doing out there on the rig. \n\nAnd when I bring it up, when I literally put the discrepancies right under their noses and say, 'Look at this, look at what you did to my chart,' they just brush me off. So, no, I'm not worried about the CIA or aliens or whatever else you might be implying. I am worried about the very real, very documented fact that my own department is using the camera system and the administrative server to systematically dismantle my career, one altered triage note at a time.
